newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-BRAVE MONTGOMERIE SET FOR ANOTHER ASSAULT ON A MAJOR.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-BRAVE MONTGOMERIE SET FOR ANOTHER ASSAULT ON A MAJOR.

text.p: If at first you don't succeed try, try again.
That's the suddenly boyish-looking Colin Montgomerie's mantra as he faces another opportunity to shed his status as the world's best player yet to win a major.

Montgomerie, who in the last six weeks has shed 17 pounds (8 kg) and about 10 years of age in his appearance, hopes to bounce back from yet another Grand Slam disappointment at the PGA Championship starting Thursday at Winged Foot.
The Briton, fifth in world rankings, was runner-up by one shot at this year's U.S. Open to Ernie Els, who also beat Montgomerie in a playoff at the 1994 U.S. Open at Oakmont.
Two years ago in the PGA Championship at Riviera, Montgomerie also lost a playoff to Steve Elkington.
"It gets tougher as they go on," Montgomerie said Wednesday. "Every time I finish second is tougher than the last. But you just keep going."
Montgomerie rededicated himself to fitness and reestablished his confidence in a double-boost at the Irish Open in Dublin, three weeks after the Open at Congressional.
"Coming back to win in Ireland was important for me," said Montgomerie, who added that he has corrected a weight shift flaw that marred his game off the tee at the British Open.
Montgomerie said he does not dwell on the disappointment of his near-misses.

"Each close call just makes me more determined than I was before," he said, mentioning that he draws inspiration from the example set by Greg Norman, who has had eight runner-up finishes in majors, including two after opponents holed-out from off the green.

"You've got to get fortunate as well as play at the top of your game. I've been in a position a number of times now when people have done something particularly good," he said. "I've been in one position when I've let it go myself.

"And I know how Greg Norman feels about people doing stuff on him, and I think he's taken it very, very well. You just have to come back and come back and come back and try. And that's what I'm doing here again. I'm trying to win."

Despite his newly gained youthful appearance, Montgomerie admits he does not qualify as a member of the emerging group of golf's young lions -- led by Masters champion Tiger Woods (21), Els (27) and British Open winner Justin Leonard (25). Nor does he consider himself one of the old guard in golf.
"I'm in the middle, really," said Montgomerie. "Hopefully I'm not the old guard. I'm 34. I'm in the middle. I'm not in the 40s, you know, the Langer, Faldo and Norman crew.

"And I'm certainly not in the 20s. So I'm in the middle. I think (Jose Maria) Olazabal and I are sort of in that middle bit. He's 32, I'm 34. So we're in that sort of middle gray area. We can still perform and yet have not had our best golf behind us.
"I feel I'm still improving. Every year I've felt I've improved as a pro. This is my 10th year and I feel I'm still improving this year."
Montgomerie is sure his best is to come, and hopefully, a major will come along with it.
